reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle in which exposure to volatile anaesthetic agents or the depolarising relaxant succinylcholine can trigger a life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis

A developing crisis shows a rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, tachycardia, muscle rigidity (sometimes masseter spasm), hyperthermia that is often a late sign, and metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis
Most susceptibility is autosomal dominant and linked to mutations in RYR1, encoding the ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel, with a minority linked to CACNA1S

Emergency management is immediate withdrawal of triggering agents, dantrolene, and aggressive supportive cooling and correction of acidosis and hyperkalaemia, alongside a switch to a trigger-free anaesthetic technique
The in-vitro (caffeine-halothane) contracture test on freshly biopsied muscle remains the diagnostic reference standard, complemented by genetic testing
Susceptibility overlaps with certain RYR1-related myopathies such as central core disease, and a personal or family history of anaesthetic death or unexplained rigidity is an important clue
Patients and relatives should carry documentation of their status and be referred to a specialist malignant hyperthermia unit for family investigation
reference.pathophysiology: Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility most often results from mutations in RYR1, the gene encoding the ryanodine receptor that releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during excitation-contraction coupling, and less often from mutations in the CACNA1S calcium channel that triggers it. The abnormal channel is hypersensitive, so on exposure to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine it releases uncontrolled calcium into the myoplasm. Sustained high calcium drives continuous muscle contraction and a runaway increase in aerobic and anaerobic metabolism, generating heat, carbon dioxide and lactate, depleting adenosine triphosphate, and causing membrane breakdown with rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Without prompt treatment this hypermetabolic cascade progresses to multi-organ failure.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis or thyroid storm causing intraoperative hyperthermia
Inadequate anaesthesia or ventilation causing hypercapnia and tachycardia
Other RYR1-related myopathies with anaesthetic sensitivity
additionalInvestigations: In-vitro contracture testing (caffeine-halothane) on freshly biopsied skeletal muscle at a specialist unit
Targeted RYR1 and CACNA1S genetic testing
Creatine kinase and myoglobin, with arterial blood gases and potassium during a suspected crisis
Electrocardiography and continuous monitoring for hyperkalaemic and acidotic changes
Muscle biopsy histology where an associated core myopathy is suspected
Detailed personal and family anaesthetic history
redFlags: Unexplained rising end-tidal carbon dioxide with tachycardia and rigidity under anaesthesia
Rapidly rising core temperature with metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia or dark myoglobinuric urine
Family history of anaesthetic death or unexplained perioperative crisis
reference.prognosis: With early recognition, prompt dantrolene and modern supportive care the mortality of an acute crisis is now low, and susceptible individuals can undergo safe anaesthesia using trigger-free agents, but an unrecognised or untreated crisis remains rapidly fatal.
pitfalls: Waiting for hyperthermia, which is frequently a late sign, before acting on rising carbon dioxide and rigidity
Confusing a crisis with neuroleptic malignant or serotonin syndrome and delaying dantrolene
Assuming a previously uneventful anaesthetic excludes susceptibility, since crises can occur on later exposures
Failing to refer the patient and family for contracture and genetic testing and to document trigger-agent avoidance
